title: Is the USPS Delivery Text a Scam? How to Spot It (2026)
meta_description: Got a text from 'USPS' about a missed delivery, address issue, or unpaid fee? Here's how to spot the scam in seconds and what to do next.
h1: Is the USPS delivery text a scam?
short_answer: Almost certainly yes. The real US Postal Service never sends unsolicited texts asking you to pay a fee, confirm an address, or click a link to redeliver a package. If you get one of these texts, it is a phishing scam — sometimes called 'smishing.' Delete it and do not tap the link.
red_flags: Text comes from a random 10-digit number or international code (real USPS uses short codes only when you've signed up)
Link points to a domain that isn't usps.com — common fakes: usps-redelivery.com, uspstracking.net, usps-pay.com
Asks you to pay a small fee (usually $1.99 – $3.95) to release a package
Creates urgency — 'within 12 hours,' 'final notice,' 'package will be returned'
You don't actually have a package coming, or the tracking number doesn't match any real USPS format

examples.message: USPS: Your package has been held due to an incomplete address. Confirm here within 12 hours or it will be returned: https://usps-redelivery.info/track
examples.reason: Real USPS domain is usps.com — never .info or hyphenated lookalikes. USPS does not hold packages over address confirmation by SMS.

examples.message: [USPS] Hi, our courier was unable to deliver your parcel. Please pay the redelivery fee of $1.99 at: uspstrack-fee.com
examples.reason: USPS does not charge redelivery fees by text. The domain is fake. The $1.99 charge exists to capture your card details — the real loss can be thousands.

what_to_do: Do not tap the link. Even opening it can fingerprint your device.
Do not reply 'STOP' — that confirms the number is active.
If you have a real package coming, go to usps.com directly and paste the tracking number there.
Report the text: forward it to 7726 (SPAM) — free on all major US carriers.
Delete the message. Block the number.
If you already tapped the link and entered card details, call your bank immediately to freeze the card.
why_scammers_use: Package delivery scams are the single most-reported text scam in the United States. Scammers send them in waves of millions because the timing is plausible — almost everyone is expecting a package from somewhere. The small fake fee ($1.99) makes the request feel low-risk to the victim, but the real goal is harvesting card numbers, names, and addresses for resale or larger fraud.

faq.q: Does USPS ever text customers?
faq.a: Only if you've explicitly signed up for Informed Delivery alerts. Even then, USPS never asks for payment, personal information, or a tap-through to a non-usps.com domain by text.

faq.q: What if the tracking number looks real?
faq.a: Scammers often paste random sequences that look like USPS tracking numbers. The only way to verify is to go to usps.com directly and search the number there — never use the link in the text.

faq.q: I already entered my address. Am I in danger?
faq.a: Your address alone is low-risk but combined with other data it can fuel future targeted scams. If you also entered card details or your SSN, call your bank and freeze your credit immediately.

title: FedEx Delivery Text Scam: How to Spot It Instantly
meta_description: FedEx delivery texts about address issues, customs fees, or held packages are usually scams. Learn the exact red flags and what to do.
h1: Is the FedEx delivery text a scam?
short_answer: Yes — almost every unsolicited 'FedEx' text asking you to pay a fee, confirm your address, or tap a link is a phishing scam. Real FedEx alerts only come if you signed up for Delivery Manager, and they never ask for payment or personal info by SMS.
red_flags: Link doesn't go to fedex.com — common fakes use fedex-redelivery, fedex-trk, fedex.shipping-status, etc.
Demands a small customs or redelivery fee, usually under $5
Sent from a regular phone number or unknown short code
Comes when you aren't expecting any international package
Spelling, capitalization, or punctuation feels slightly off — 'Fedex' instead of 'FedEx,' missing periods

examples.message: FedEx: Parcel #8839271 held — customs fee of $3.50 required. Pay now to release: https://fedex-trk.com/customs
examples.reason: FedEx does not collect customs fees by text. The domain is not fedex.com. Customs fees, when real, are collected at delivery in person or by registered mail.

examples.message: [FedEx Notice] You have an outstanding delivery. Reschedule here: fedex.shipping-status.net/u
examples.reason: The actual domain is shipping-status.net, not fedex.com. 'fedex' before the dot is meaningless — it's just the subdomain of a fake site.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link.
If expecting a real shipment, go to fedex.com directly and use your real tracking number from the seller's confirmation email.
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) to report it to your carrier.
Delete and block. Don't reply 'STOP.'
If you tapped the link and entered information, call your bank to freeze the card and consider a credit freeze.
why_scammers_use: Shipping scams work because they hit at the right moment — we're all expecting something. The customs-fee variant exploits the fact that most people have only a vague understanding of how international shipping fees work, so a small dollar amount feels plausible.

faq.q: Does FedEx collect customs fees by text?
faq.a: No. Real customs duties are collected by your carrier at delivery (cash or card to the driver) or by mail after delivery. Never by an unsolicited SMS link.

faq.q: The text knows my name. Is it still a scam?
faq.a: Yes. Names are widely available from data leaks. A personalized text is not proof of legitimacy — many large scam operations now buy lists with name + phone pairs.

title: Amazon Refund Scam: Email, Text & Call Red Flags
meta_description: Got a message about an unexpected Amazon refund, charge, or order you didn't make? Here's how to tell if it's a scam — and what to do.
h1: Is the Amazon refund / charge message a scam?
short_answer: Yes, in 99% of cases. Unsolicited emails, texts, or calls about a 'refund,' 'order you didn't place,' or 'charge to verify' are phishing — designed to get you to call a fake support line or hand over your password. Real Amazon never asks you to confirm orders by reading a code or installing 'support software.'
red_flags: Lists an expensive item you didn't buy (iPhone, MacBook, gold bars) — designed to make you panic and call
Includes a phone number to 'cancel' or 'dispute' — that number connects to scammers
Email sender is not @amazon.com (look at the full address, not the display name)
Asks you to install 'remote support' software like AnyDesk or TeamViewer
Refund process requires you to read out a verification code, gift card numbers, or buy gift cards

examples.message: Amazon Order Confirmation #207-4839201: iPhone 16 Pro Max ($1,299.00). To cancel or dispute this charge, call 1-888-555-0143 within 24 hours.
examples.reason: Amazon does not include a phone number to 'cancel' in order confirmations. The order shock is bait — when you call, scammers will walk you through 'refunding' by sending them gift cards or installing remote access software.

examples.message: This is Amazon support. We see suspicious activity on your account. To protect your funds, please move your money to a 'secure account' while we investigate.
examples.reason: Amazon will never call you about account security and certainly never asks you to move money. 'Move to a secure account' is a wire fraud script — the secure account is the scammer's account.

what_to_do: Do not call the number in the message.
Open the Amazon app or go to amazon.com directly. Check 'Your Orders' — if there's nothing there, the message is fake.
If a real order is there that you didn't place, report it through Amazon's Message Center, not by phone.
Never install remote-control software at the request of 'support' — it gives them full access to your bank.
If you already gave them money or gift cards: report to your bank immediately and file at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
why_scammers_use: The fake Amazon refund is the most common 'callback' scam in North America. Showing a $1,200+ purchase triggers panic, and panicked people call numbers. Once on the phone, scammers spend 30–90 minutes walking the victim through 'fixing' the charge — almost always ending with the victim buying thousands of dollars of gift cards 'to refund themselves.'

faq.q: Does Amazon ever call about orders?
faq.a: Extremely rarely, and only in response to a request you made. Amazon does not cold-call about charges. If you're unsure, hang up and check the app.

faq.q: I called and they had my name and address. Is it real?
faq.a: No. Scammers buy data from leaks. Knowing your name doesn't make a caller legitimate.

title: IRS Scam Texts and Calls: How to Identify Them in 2026
meta_description: The IRS never texts, never threatens arrest by phone, and never demands gift cards. Here's exactly how to spot and report IRS impersonation scams.
h1: Is the IRS text or call a scam?
short_answer: Yes — every unsolicited IRS text or threatening phone call is a scam. The real IRS contacts taxpayers by US mail first, never by SMS, never by email, and never demands immediate payment in gift cards, wire, or cryptocurrency. If someone claiming to be the IRS contacts you any other way, it's an impersonator.
red_flags: Threatens immediate arrest, deportation, or license suspension
Demands payment in gift cards, wire transfer, cryptocurrency, or prepaid debit cards
Text or email — IRS does not contact taxpayers this way for first contact
Caller ID 'spoofed' to show 'IRS' or a Washington DC number
Refuses to give you a callback number or pin to verify through irs.gov

examples.message: This is Officer Johnson with the Internal Revenue Service. A warrant has been issued for your arrest for unpaid taxes. To avoid imprisonment, you must pay $2,847 in Apple gift cards within the next hour.
examples.reason: The IRS does not arrest people for unpaid taxes by phone, does not accept gift cards as payment, and never gives one-hour deadlines. Every element is fake.

examples.message: IRS Tax Refund Notice: You are eligible for a refund of $1,847.30. Click here to claim within 24 hours: irs-refund-claim.us
examples.reason: The IRS does not email refunds. The real domain is irs.gov — anything else is a fake. The link harvests SSNs, bank info, and identity data.

what_to_do: Hang up immediately if it's a call. Do not engage, do not press any numbers.
Do not click any link in IRS-themed emails or texts.
If you owe taxes (or think you might), check directly at irs.gov by logging into your account.
Report IRS phone scams to TIGTA at tigta.gov/reportcrime or 1-800-366-4484.
Forward suspicious IRS-themed emails to phishing@irs.gov.
If you paid: call your bank, file a police report, and report at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
why_scammers_use: IRS scams exploit the universal fear of tax trouble. Victims are often older adults or recent immigrants — both groups statistically more likely to trust authority and less familiar with how the IRS actually operates. Gift-card payment is preferred by scammers because it's untraceable and irreversible once redeemed.

faq.q: How does the IRS actually contact people?
faq.a: First contact is almost always by physical US mail. The IRS may follow up by phone after mail contact, but never demands immediate payment over the phone.

faq.q: The caller knew my last four digits of SSN. Is that proof?
faq.a: No. Partial SSNs are widely leaked. A scammer with your last four is not the IRS.

title: Social Security Scam Calls: Suspended SSN & How to Spot Them
meta_description: Got a call saying your Social Security number is suspended or linked to a crime? It's a scam. Here's exactly how to recognize and report it.
h1: Is the 'Social Security suspended' call a scam?
short_answer: Yes — 100% of the time. Your Social Security number cannot be 'suspended,' 'blocked,' or 'frozen.' That's not a thing. Any call telling you otherwise is a criminal impersonator, no exceptions.
red_flags: Robocall or 'agent' saying your SSN is suspended, frozen, or linked to crimes
Claims your SSN was used in money laundering, drug trafficking, or a rental car in Texas
Tells you to press 1 to speak to an officer
Demands you 'verify' your full SSN by reading it back
Tells you to withdraw cash, buy gift cards, or convert to crypto to 'protect' your money

examples.message: This call is from the Social Security Administration. Your Social Security number has been suspended due to suspicious activity. Press 1 to speak with an officer immediately or face legal action.
examples.reason: SSA does not robocall, cannot suspend SSNs (it's not technically possible), and does not threaten legal action by phone. Every part of this script is fake.

examples.message: Hello, I'm Officer Sarah Mills, badge 4419, with Social Security. Your SSN has been linked to a vehicle abandoned at the Texas border with $20,000 cash. We need to verify your identity to clear your name.
examples.reason: SSA officers don't have badge numbers, don't investigate border crimes, and don't ask you to 'verify identity' by phone. Classic impersonation script.

what_to_do: Hang up. Do not press 1 — that flags you as a live target.
Never read your SSN to anyone who called you.
If you're worried about your SSN, call SSA directly at 1-800-772-1213 (do not use a number a caller gave you).
Report the call at oig.ssa.gov/report.
Place a free credit freeze at all three bureaus (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) if you gave any data.
why_scammers_use: The 'suspended SSN' scam is one of the longest-running US phone scams because it's so effective on older adults — who tend to take official-sounding calls seriously. The threat of crime + immediate fear creates a 'panic window' where victims act without thinking.

faq.q: Can my Social Security number be suspended?
faq.a: No. SSNs are not suspended, frozen, or cancelled. That concept does not exist.

faq.q: Does SSA ever call people?
faq.a: Yes, but only after a written letter, and only if you have an ongoing case. They will never threaten arrest or demand immediate action.

title: Medicare Cancellation Scam: Texts, Calls & Cards
meta_description: Got a call or text saying your Medicare coverage will be cancelled? It's a scam. Learn how to spot it and protect yourself.
h1: Is the Medicare cancellation message a scam?
short_answer: Yes. Medicare does not cancel your coverage by text or unsolicited phone call. Medicare communicates by mail. Any caller asking to 'verify' your Medicare number, send a new card, or warn of cancellation is an impersonator — usually trying to steal your Medicare ID to file fraudulent claims.
red_flags: Caller asks for your Medicare number 'to verify your account'
Offers a 'new plastic Medicare card' or 'free upgrade'
Text claims your coverage will be cancelled if you don't act today
Asks for your bank or credit card to 'cover the cost' of a new benefit
Pressures you to switch Medicare plans by phone immediately

examples.message: Your Medicare coverage will be cancelled on March 15. Call 1-800-555-4499 now to verify your information.
examples.reason: Medicare never cancels coverage by text and never asks you to call an unverified number. Real coverage changes come by mail with at least 30 days' notice.

examples.message: Hello, this is Medicare. We're sending you a new plastic card — much better than the paper one. Can you confirm your Medicare number so we can update it?
examples.reason: Medicare did not switch to 'plastic cards.' Real Medicare cards are paper. Anyone asking for your Medicare number is trying to bill fraudulent claims under your account.

what_to_do: Hang up or delete the message.
Never give your Medicare number to anyone who called you.
If you have questions, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) directly — never the number from the message.
Report Medicare fraud at 1-800-HHS-TIPS (1-800-447-8477).
Sign up for your Medicare summary notices online at medicare.gov to spot fraudulent claims early.
why_scammers_use: Medicare numbers are extremely valuable on the dark market — they let fraudsters bill the government for fake medical procedures. A single stolen Medicare ID can be worth thousands in fraudulent billing. Scammers target older adults knowing the urgency around medical coverage drives quick, emotional responses.

faq.q: How will Medicare contact me about real changes?
faq.a: By mail. Always by mail first. If something seems urgent, call 1-800-MEDICARE to verify.

faq.q: Are the 'free knee brace' or 'free back brace' calls also scams?
faq.a: Yes. These are durable-medical-equipment Medicare fraud schemes. Hang up and report at 1-800-HHS-TIPS.

title: Geek Squad Renewal Scam: Fake $399 Invoice Emails
meta_description: Got an email about a Geek Squad renewal you didn't sign up for? It's a phishing scam. Here's how to spot it and what to do.
h1: Is the Geek Squad renewal email a scam?
short_answer: Yes. The 'Geek Squad auto-renewal' invoice is one of the most common phishing emails in circulation. Best Buy / Geek Squad does not auto-renew old subscriptions you forgot about — and they don't send these emails. The fake invoice exists to make you call a 'support number' where scammers steal your money.
red_flags: Invoice for an amount like $349.99, $399.99, or $499.99 — designed to look like a real subscription
Email lists a phone number to 'cancel' the charge — that's the scam's hook
Sender address is not @bestbuy.com or @geeksquad.com
PDF attachment with the same fake invoice — designed to bypass spam filters
Says renewal happens in 24–48 hours if you don't act

examples.message: Geek Squad Auto-Renewal Confirmation. Your Total Tech Protection plan has been renewed for $389.99. If you didn't authorize this, call 1-855-555-0192 to cancel within 24 hours.
examples.reason: Geek Squad doesn't send confirmation emails with a 'call to cancel' number. Calling connects you to scammers who walk you through installing remote-access software to 'refund' you — they'll actually drain your bank.

examples.message: Invoice #INV-78491 attached. Renewal of Geek Squad Premium Tech Support: $399.99. Questions? Call our billing team at 1-844-555-0288.
examples.reason: The PDF attachment is bait — the real attack is the phone number. Once you call, scammers will get you on a remote-access session and drain accounts.

what_to_do: Do not call the number in the email.
Do not open the PDF.
Check your actual bank/credit card statements for a real charge from Best Buy — there won't be one.
If you ever did have a Geek Squad subscription, log into bestbuy.com directly to check.
Report the phishing email — forward to reportphishing@apwg.org.
Delete the email. Block the sender.
why_scammers_use: Geek Squad has millions of customers, so a random recipient has a non-zero chance of being a real subscriber — that ambiguity drives the panic call. The $399 figure is high enough to alarm but low enough that a victim feels they can 'just call to fix it.' Once on the phone, the scam unfolds over an hour and ends in major financial loss.

faq.q: What if I really do have a Geek Squad subscription?
faq.a: Log into bestbuy.com directly (not via the email) to verify. Real billing issues are visible in your account.

faq.q: I opened the PDF. Did I infect my computer?
faq.a: Most likely no — these PDFs are usually just the image of the invoice. But if you clicked any link inside, run a virus scan and change your email password.

title: Norton Renewal Scam: Fake LifeLock Invoice Emails
meta_description: Got an unexpected Norton or LifeLock renewal email for $300+? It's almost certainly a phishing scam. Here's how to identify it.
h1: Is the Norton / LifeLock renewal email a scam?
short_answer: Yes, in almost all cases. Norton (and its sister product LifeLock) do not send unsolicited 'auto-renewal' emails with phone numbers to call. The real Norton manages renewals through your account dashboard. The fake invoice is bait — the goal is to get you on the phone with a scammer.
red_flags: Lists a renewal amount around $299, $349, or $499 — high enough to alarm
Email includes a phone number to 'cancel' — the scam's trap
Sender domain is not @norton.com or @nortonlifelock.com
Subject line uses urgent language: 'Final Notice,' 'Auto-Renewal Confirmed'
PDF or image attachment mimicking an invoice

examples.message: Norton 360 LifeLock Auto-Renewal: $349.99 charged to your account. Cancel within 24 hours by calling +1-833-555-0117.
examples.reason: Norton does not include a phone-to-cancel link in renewal emails. Real renewal disputes go through norton.com support. The phone number routes to fraud operators.

what_to_do: Don't call the number.
Check your real card statement — there won't be a Norton charge.
If unsure, log into norton.com directly to see your subscription status.
Report the email to spam@nortonlifelock.com.
Delete the message.
why_scammers_use: Norton is a recognized brand with millions of customers — same playbook as Geek Squad. Fake invoices for $300+ trigger immediate emotional response, and the call is where the real fraud happens.

faq.q: What if I actually have Norton?
faq.a: Log into your account at norton.com directly. Real renewals are visible there, and you can cancel from inside your account — never by a phone number from an email.

title: 'Your Apple ID Has Been Locked' Scam: How to Spot It
meta_description: Got a text, email, or call saying your Apple ID is locked or suspended? It's a phishing scam. Learn how to identify and report it.
h1: Is the 'Apple ID locked' message a scam?
short_answer: Yes. Apple does not send unsolicited texts or emails saying your Apple ID is locked, suspended, or compromised. The real Apple manages account issues inside your device's Settings or via appleid.apple.com. The 'locked Apple ID' message is one of the highest-volume phishing attacks in the world.
red_flags: Link goes to a domain that isn't apple.com (apple-support-id.com, appleid-verify.net, etc.)
Asks you to 'verify your password' or 'reconfirm payment information' via a link
Sender is not @apple.com (look at the full address, not the display name)
Threatens account closure in 24–48 hours
Asks you to read a verification code sent to your phone

examples.message: Apple Support: Your Apple ID has been locked due to unusual activity. Verify your identity here within 24 hours: appleid-secure.com
examples.reason: The real domain is apple.com or appleid.apple.com — never appleid-secure.com or similar. Tapping the link leads to a fake login page that captures your Apple ID password.

examples.message: This is Apple Support. We've detected someone in Russia logging into your iCloud. To secure your account, please read the 6-digit code we just sent to your phone.
examples.reason: Apple does not call about iCloud breaches. The code they're asking for is the 2FA code that lets THEM into your account. Never read a 2FA code to anyone who called you.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link or read the code.
If worried, check your Apple ID directly: Settings > [Your Name] on your iPhone, or appleid.apple.com in a browser you type yourself.
Forward phishing emails to reportphishing@apple.com.
Forward phishing texts to 7726 (SPAM).
If you already entered your password on a fake site: immediately change it at appleid.apple.com and enable two-factor authentication.
why_scammers_use: Almost everyone has an Apple ID, which makes this scam plausible to ~70% of recipients. A stolen Apple ID gives access to iCloud photos, contacts, payment methods, and Find My — extremely valuable to criminals.

faq.q: What does a real Apple security alert look like?
faq.a: It appears as a notification on your Apple device itself, not as a text or email. Real alerts let you 'Review' from inside Settings.

faq.q: I tapped the link but didn't enter anything. Am I safe?
faq.a: Probably yes. Just tapping a link doesn't compromise your account. Don't return to the link, and don't tap it again.

title: Grandparent Scam: Fake Emergency Calls Targeting Seniors
meta_description: A panicked call from 'your grandchild' in trouble is almost always a scam. Learn the script, the red flags, and how to respond.
h1: Is the 'grandchild in trouble' call a scam?
short_answer: Yes — almost certainly. The grandparent scam (also called the 'family emergency scam') is one of the cruelest and fastest-growing phone frauds. A caller pretends to be a grandchild in jail, in a car accident, or stranded abroad, and demands urgent cash, gift cards, or wire transfer. Real emergencies don't sound like this script.
red_flags: Caller says 'Grandma? Grandpa?' and waits for you to fill in the name
Voice sounds 'a bit off' — they'll blame it on injury, a cold, or a broken nose
Begs you not to tell their parents
Demands cash, gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency
A second caller pretends to be a lawyer, police officer, or bail bondsman
Asks you to meet a 'courier' in person to hand over cash — newest variant

examples.message: Grandma? It's me. I'm in trouble. I was in a car accident and I'm in jail. Please don't tell Mom. My lawyer will call you in a minute — you need to wire $5,000 to pay my bail.
examples.reason: Real arrests don't work this way. No US jail demands wire transfers or gift cards for bail. The 'don't tell Mom' line is specifically designed to isolate the victim from anyone who would spot the scam.

examples.message: [Voice that sounds exactly like grandchild]: Grandma, I'm in trouble. I need help. Please, don't ask questions, just send the money.
examples.reason: Scammers now use AI to clone a grandchild's voice from a few seconds of social media audio. If you hear this, stay calm, hang up, and call the real grandchild's known number to verify.

what_to_do: Stay calm. Don't say any names — let them try to fill in the gap.
Hang up.
Call the real grandchild directly on their known number — not any number the caller gave you.
Call their parents to verify.
Set up a family code word for real emergencies — a word only family knows. Use it whenever something feels off.
Report at reportfraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general's consumer protection unit.
If you already sent money: call your bank immediately. Cash-by-courier variants can sometimes be intercepted if you act within an hour.
why_scammers_use: This scam targets emotion, not logic. The combination of panic, secrecy, and urgency overrides the rational checks an older adult would normally do. AI voice cloning has made the scam dramatically more convincing in the past two years — even very alert seniors have lost six-figure sums.

faq.q: My grandchild's voice sounded real. Are you sure it's a scam?
faq.a: AI voice cloning can replicate any voice from a 10-second sample. Always hang up and call back on a number you know.

faq.q: What's a good family code word?
faq.a: Something memorable but not guessable from social media — not a pet name, not a hometown. A favorite childhood food, an inside joke, an unusual word.

title: Chase Fraud Alert Text Scam: How to Tell Real from Fake
meta_description: Got a text from 'Chase' about a charge or fraud alert? Some are real, most are scams. Here's exactly how to tell.
h1: Is the Chase fraud alert text a scam?
short_answer: Often, yes. Real Chase fraud alerts ask you to reply YES or NO — they never include a link, never ask you to call a number in the message, and never ask for your full account number, password, or PIN. If the text has any of those, it's a phishing scam.
red_flags: Includes a link to tap (real Chase alerts use SMS short codes and no links)
Asks you to call a phone number that isn't on the back of your Chase card
Asks for your full account number, password, PIN, or 2FA code
Sender is a regular 10-digit number (real Chase uses short codes like 24273 or 96632)
Threatens immediate account closure

examples.message: CHASE ALERT: A charge of $487.22 at Best Buy was attempted. If unauthorized, call 1-855-555-0148 immediately to dispute.
examples.reason: Real Chase alerts ask you to reply YES or NO — never to call a number embedded in the message. The fake number routes to scammers who 'help' you 'move money to a safe account' (theirs).

examples.message: FREE MSG: Chase Fraud - Did you charge $52.18 at Shell Oil on 3/14? Reply YES, NO, or HELP.
examples.reason: This is a real Chase fraud alert format — uses a short code, asks for a simple YES/NO reply, no link, no callback number. Replying YES or NO is safe.

what_to_do: If the text has a link or callback number, ignore both.
Open the Chase app directly or call the number on the back of your Chase card.
If you've already tapped a link and entered credentials, call Chase immediately at 1-800-935-9935 and change your password.
Forward the suspicious text to 7726.
Block the sender.
why_scammers_use: Bank fraud alerts have built up trust — people are used to receiving real ones and tend to act on them quickly. Scammers piggyback on that trust. The 'call this number' variant typically leads to a 30-minute social engineering call ending in wire transfers or remote-access account drain.

faq.q: How does a real Chase fraud alert look?
faq.a: A short code (5-digit sender), a question about a specific charge, and asks you to reply YES, NO, or HELP. No links, no phone numbers in the message itself.

faq.q: I replied to a fake one. Am I in trouble?
faq.a: Replying just confirms your number is active — it's not catastrophic. But don't tap any follow-up link, and call Chase directly to be safe.

title: Zelle Scams: How They Work and How to Avoid Them
meta_description: Zelle transfers are instant and irreversible — which is exactly why scammers love them. Learn the most common Zelle scams and how to spot them.
h1: How do Zelle scams work?
short_answer: Zelle scams work because Zelle payments are instant and almost impossible to reverse. Scammers trick victims into 'sending money to themselves' through Zelle — which is actually sending it to the scammer. Banks rarely refund Zelle fraud because the transfer was 'authorized' by you, even when you were tricked.
red_flags: Caller says they're from your bank's 'fraud department' and instructs you to send a Zelle to 'yourself' or to 'verify' an account
Asks you to read a Zelle confirmation code aloud
Marketplace seller (Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace) insists on Zelle for a 'deposit' before showing the item
Anyone instructs you to use Zelle to 'reverse' a fraudulent charge
Pressure to send money in 5–10 minutes

examples.message: This is the Wells Fargo fraud team. We've detected unauthorized Zelle activity. To protect your funds, please send a Zelle to yourself for $2,500 — this will lock the account.
examples.reason: Banks never instruct you to send Zelle to yourself. There's no such thing as 'locking' an account by Zelle. The recipient is the scammer, who has set up a name that matches yours.

examples.message: Hi, I'm interested in the couch. To hold it, can you send a $200 Zelle deposit? I'll pick up tomorrow.
examples.reason: Reverse direction of normal scams — here the 'buyer' is trying to get YOU to send Zelle, which they'll claim was wrong and demand back. Never accept Zelle from strangers on marketplace listings.

what_to_do: Never send Zelle to anyone you don't personally know.
If 'your bank' calls about fraud, hang up and call the number on the back of your card.
Banks will never ask you to move money to 'yourself' to 'protect' it.
If you've been scammed: file a fraud report with your bank within 24 hours, file at reportfraud.ftc.gov, and file at ic3.gov.
Treat Zelle like cash — once sent, it's gone.
why_scammers_use: Zelle was designed for trusted person-to-person transfers and lacks the fraud protections of credit cards. Once a Zelle transfer completes, the money is in the recipient's account in seconds and can be withdrawn or moved before fraud is even reported. Banks lean on the 'you authorized it' defense to refuse refunds.

faq.q: Can I get my Zelle money back?
faq.a: Sometimes, if you act within 24 hours and the recipient hasn't withdrawn — but banks are not legally required to refund Zelle scams, and most don't.

faq.q: What's safer than Zelle for online payments?
faq.a: Credit cards (full chargeback protection). For person-to-person with someone you know, Zelle is fine — but never with strangers.

title: Romance Scams: How to Recognize the Patterns
meta_description: Online romance turning into money requests? Here's how to spot a romance scam, why it works, and what to do if you're already involved.
h1: Is this online relationship a romance scam?
short_answer: If someone you met online has never met you in person, professes love quickly, and is now asking for money — it is almost certainly a romance scam. Romance scams are the highest-loss fraud category in the US, costing victims an average of $15,000 each. The relationship is real to you. To them, it's a script.
red_flags: Met online (dating app, Facebook, Instagram, even WhatsApp DM)
Has never video-called you — or 'video calls' are very short with poor quality
Says 'I love you' within days or weeks
Profession that conveniently keeps them away: military deployed abroad, oil rig worker, doctor abroad with WHO
Eventually asks for money — for an emergency, a flight to visit you, a stuck shipment, customs fees, medical bills
Sob stories escalate over time
Will not meet in person no matter what
Photos look 'too good' — often stolen from real social media profiles

examples.message: My darling, I'm finally coming to see you next week. But my company won't release my last paycheck until I pay $4,500 in fees. Can you help me, my love? I'll pay you back the moment I land.
examples.reason: No real company holds final pay hostage with fees. No real visa or travel system requires the visitor's lover to send money. This is the most common variant — used millions of times globally.

examples.message: I've been making great returns on this crypto platform. Let me show you — start with $500, you'll see the gains in a week. My uncle works there, he gave me access.
examples.reason: Pig butchering: the relationship is the long con to set up the investment scam. The 'platform' is a fake site that shows fake gains. When you try to withdraw, fees keep being added until you give up — and the money is gone.

what_to_do: If you haven't sent money yet: do a reverse image search of their photos (Google Images, TinEye) — you'll usually find the real person elsewhere.
Ask for a live video call right now. Real people can. Scammers can't, or use deepfakes that fail under questioning.
If you've sent money: stop sending immediately. The relationship is not real. No future money will bring them to you.
Tell someone you trust — scammers depend on isolation. Saying it out loud breaks the spell for many victims.
Report at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov.
If you sent crypto: report immediately to ic3.gov. There's a small chance of recovery if reported within days.
why_scammers_use: Romance scams have the highest per-victim losses of any fraud category because the relationship is real to the victim. Scammers are trained, follow scripts, and run multiple 'relationships' simultaneously. Many are themselves victims of human trafficking, forced to run scams from compounds in Southeast Asia. The 'pig butchering' (investment) variant is now a multi-billion-dollar industry.

faq.q: But what if it really is true love?
faq.a: If it's real, they can wait. Anyone who pressures you for money over an online-only relationship is not a partner — they are a scammer or a desperate person. Real partners do not ask for thousands of dollars from someone they've never met.

faq.q: I've sent so much. Can I get it back?
faq.a: Usually no, but always file reports — at ic3.gov, your local police, and the platform where you met. Some funds can be traced. And contact a fraud counselor; the emotional damage is significant.

title: Pig Butchering Scam: The Long-Con Crypto Trap
meta_description: Pig butchering combines romance and fake crypto investments to drain entire savings. Here's how to recognize and avoid it.
h1: What is a 'pig butchering' scam?
short_answer: Pig butchering ('shā zhū pán' in Chinese) is a long-con scam combining romance, friendship, or business mentorship with fake cryptocurrency investments. Scammers spend weeks or months building trust, then introduce a 'great investment opportunity' on a fake trading platform. Victims see fake gains, invest more, and lose everything when they try to withdraw.
red_flags: Unexpected message from a stranger on WhatsApp, Telegram, dating apps, or LinkedIn
Quickly moves the conversation to a private app like WhatsApp or Telegram
Talks about their 'amazing' crypto investments or has an 'uncle' / 'mentor' in finance
Eventually invites you to a trading platform — often with a sleek interface that mimics real exchanges
Small initial deposits show real gains (the platform is fake; the numbers are made up)
When you try to withdraw a profit, you're told to pay 'taxes,' 'release fees,' or 'identity verification' first
Pressure to put in more — house equity, retirement savings, loans from family

examples.message: Hi, sorry — I think I have the wrong number. But you seem nice. I'm Emily, I just moved to LA for work. What about you?
examples.reason: The 'wrong number' opener is a global standard pig-butchering script. The 'Emily' moves to a long chat that eventually pivots to investments. Block immediately.

examples.message: Congratulations, your account is now $87,000. To withdraw, you need to pay 15% capital gains tax ($13,050) to the platform. Once that's paid, your withdrawal will be released.
examples.reason: Real exchanges deduct taxes from your withdrawal — they never require you to send additional money to withdraw your own. This is the final extraction phase: scammers keep inventing fees until victims run out of money.

what_to_do: If you got a 'wrong number' DM from a stranger that became a friendly chat: block them. That's the whole scam.
If you're in one: stop sending money. Do not pay the 'release fee' — the money is gone, and paying more will not recover it.
Tell a trusted friend or family member. Pig butchering depends on isolation.
Report to ic3.gov immediately — early reporting occasionally enables crypto trace and freeze.
Save all messages and screenshots before the scammer goes dark.
Talk to a fraud counselor — AARP's fraud hotline (1-877-908-3360) and the Cybercrime Support Network (cybercrimesupport.org) offer free help.
why_scammers_use: Pig butchering is now the largest single category of online fraud globally. Operations run from large compounds (mostly in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos) where workers — often trafficked themselves — follow scripts to build relationships and 'butcher the pig' (drain the victim). Average loss per victim is over $100,000.

faq.q: The platform shows my money is still there. Why can't I withdraw?
faq.a: The platform is fake. Those numbers are not real. You don't have any money there. Sending more 'release fees' makes the problem worse.

faq.q: Can I get any of it back?
faq.a: Very rarely. Quick reports to ic3.gov give the best chance. Some private firms claim crypto recovery but most are themselves scams — be extremely careful.

title: Car Warranty Robocall Scam: 'Your Vehicle's Warranty Has Expired'
meta_description: Getting calls about your car's expired warranty? They're scams. Here's how to identify and stop them.
h1: Is the 'car warranty expired' call a scam?
short_answer: Yes. The 'extended car warranty' robocall is almost always a scam. Even when a real extended warranty is offered, it's often a high-pressure sales scam that takes money for coverage that will never pay claims. The robocallers don't know what car you own — they just call millions of numbers hoping someone bites.
red_flags: Robocall starts with 'this is your final notice about your vehicle's warranty'
Has no idea what car you own — and avoids saying it
Press 1 to speak with a 'specialist'
Demands payment by credit card on the call
Refuses to send paperwork before payment
Claims to be from 'your dealership' or 'the manufacturer'

examples.message: This is your final notice. Our records indicate your vehicle's warranty has expired or is about to expire. Press 1 now to speak with a specialist and extend your coverage.
examples.reason: Real car manufacturers and dealerships don't robocall about warranty status. This is a sales scam designed to extract credit card details under pressure for a worthless 'service contract.'

what_to_do: Hang up. Do not press any number — pressing 1 confirms your number and triggers more calls.
If you want a real extended warranty, contact your dealership or manufacturer directly.
Register your number on the National Do Not Call Registry at donotcall.gov (though scammers ignore it).
Report the call at donotcall.gov/report.
Use your phone's built-in call blocking (iPhone: Settings > Phone > Silence Unknown Callers).
why_scammers_use: Auto-dialing technology makes mass calls almost free. Even a 0.1% conversion rate on millions of calls is profitable. Many victims are older adults who once had a real extended warranty and find the script plausible.

faq.q: Are any extended car warranties legit?
faq.a: Yes — bought directly from a manufacturer or a reputable third party at the time of purchase. But no real provider cold-calls customers via robocall.

faq.q: How do I stop the calls?
faq.a: Honestly, you mostly can't. Block individual numbers, use 'Silence Unknown Callers' on iPhone, and use a call-screening app. Robocallers spoof numbers, so blocking is whack-a-mole.

title: UPS Delivery Text Scam: Is the Tracking Message Real?
meta_description: Got a UPS text about a missed delivery, customs fee, or address update? Most are scams. Here's how to tell, and what to do.
h1: Is the UPS delivery text a scam?
short_answer: In almost every case, yes. Real UPS only sends SMS updates if you've signed up for UPS My Choice, and they never charge fees, request address confirmation, or ask you to tap a link to a non-ups.com domain. The 'UPS' delivery text scam is one of the most-circulated smishing attacks worldwide.
red_flags: Link doesn't point to ups.com — fakes use ups-track.com, upsdelivery.net, ups-redelivery.info
Asks for a small fee ($1-5) to release or redeliver a package
Sender is a regular 10-digit number, not a UPS short code
Arrives when you have no real UPS shipment in progress
Pressures with 'within 24 hours' or 'final notice' language

examples.message: UPS: Your package #1Z9847291 could not be delivered. Confirm your address and pay the $2.99 redelivery fee: ups-redelivery.info/r/1Z
examples.reason: UPS never charges redelivery fees by text. The domain is fake. The tracking number is a plausible-looking but random sequence.

examples.message: UPS Alert: Customs inspection requires a $4.50 fee to release your parcel. Pay at: upstrack.shipping-fee.com
examples.reason: Customs fees are collected by your carrier at delivery, never by SMS. The domain is shipping-fee.com — 'upstrack' is just a meaningless subdomain.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link.
If you have a real UPS shipment, go to ups.com directly and paste your real tracking number from the sender's email.
Forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) — your carrier will investigate.
Block the sender. Delete the message.
If you tapped the link and entered card details, call your bank immediately and freeze the card.
why_scammers_use: Package-delivery smishing dominates global SMS scam volume because the timing is plausible — millions of people have an active package at any moment. Small fee asks ($1-5) feel low-risk, but the real prize is your card number for resale or larger fraud.

faq.q: Does UPS ever text customers?
faq.a: Only if you've explicitly opted into UPS My Choice notifications. Even then, they never request payment or tap-throughs by SMS.

faq.q: The text has my real name. Is that proof?
faq.a: No. Names tied to phone numbers are widely available from data leaks. Personalization is not legitimacy.

title: DHL Customs Fee Scam: Email & Text Red Flags
meta_description: Got an email or text from 'DHL' demanding a customs fee to release your package? It's a phishing scam — here's how to spot and avoid it.
h1: Is the DHL customs fee message a scam?
short_answer: Yes, in nearly all cases. Real DHL collects customs and duties through formal channels — typically at delivery, in person, or via a properly invoiced bill of lading. An unsolicited email or text asking for a small payment to 'release customs hold' is a phishing scam.
red_flags: Demands a small fee ($2-15) to release a held package
Sender domain is not dhl.com (look at the full From address, not the display name)
Links go to dhl-customs.info, dhl-pay.net, or similar lookalikes
Threatens that the package will be 'returned to sender' or 'destroyed' if unpaid
You weren't expecting an international shipment

examples.message: DHL Express — Customs hold for parcel DH-7748291. Pay €4.50 customs duty within 48 hours to release. Pay here: dhl-customs.eu/release
examples.reason: DHL collects real duties at delivery, by certified mail, or through a customs broker — never by an emailed link asking for under €15.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link or open attachments.
If a real shipment is in transit, verify by typing dhl.com into your browser and entering the tracking number from the sender's official confirmation.
Forward suspicious emails to phishing-dpdhl@dhl.com.
Delete the message. Block the sender.
If you paid, call your bank to dispute and freeze the card.
why_scammers_use: International shipping fees are confusing for most consumers, making the small 'customs fee' ask feel plausible. The under-€20 amount is below most fraud-detection thresholds and feels too small to question.

faq.q: Are any DHL fee emails real?
faq.a: Real DHL fee notices typically come from your customs broker, are tied to a known shipment, and never use shortened or unfamiliar domains.

title: 'Your Amazon Account Has Been Suspended' Email Scam
meta_description: Got an Amazon email saying your account is locked or suspended? It's a phishing trap. Here's how to spot it and what to do.
h1: Is the 'Amazon account suspended' email a scam?
short_answer: Yes. Amazon does not lock or suspend customer accounts via email and ask you to re-verify by tapping a link. These emails are phishing — designed to capture your Amazon login, which gives scammers access to your saved cards, order history, and address book.
red_flags: Sender is not @amazon.com (check full address — display names are forged)
Link goes to amazon-secure.com, amazon-verify.net, amazonid.com, or other lookalikes
Subject line uses urgent words: 'Final notice,' 'Action required,' 'Within 24 hours'
Asks you to 'verify' password, card, or full SSN
Threatens account deletion if you don't act

examples.message: Amazon Security: We've detected unusual activity. Your account has been temporarily suspended. Verify your information here to regain access: amazon-secure-verify.com
examples.reason: Real Amazon security flags appear inside the Amazon app or website — never via an email link to a non-amazon.com domain. The verify page is a perfect replica designed to steal your password.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link.
Open the Amazon app or go to amazon.com directly and log in. Real account issues are visible in 'Your Account.'
Forward the phishing email to stop-spoofing@amazon.com.
If you tapped and entered your password, change it immediately at amazon.com and enable two-factor authentication.
Check 'Login activity' in your Amazon account settings.
why_scammers_use: Amazon credentials are extremely valuable on the dark web — they typically include saved payment methods, shipping addresses, and order history. Stolen accounts are used for fraudulent purchases shipped to drop addresses.

faq.q: How does real Amazon notify of account issues?
faq.a: In-app and on-site notifications. They never link out to non-amazon.com domains for verification.

title: PayPal 'Payment Pending' Email Scam: How to Spot It
meta_description: Received a PayPal email about a pending payment, invoice, or unauthorized charge? Most are scams. Here's how to identify and avoid them.
h1: Is the PayPal payment pending email a scam?
short_answer: Likely yes. Common PayPal scams send fake invoices, fake payment-pending notices, or fake unauthorized-charge warnings — all aimed at getting you to call a fake support number or click a link that steals your login. Real PayPal activity is always visible inside the PayPal app or website.
red_flags: Includes a phone number to 'cancel' a pending transaction — the trap
Sender is not @paypal.com (check full address)
Email is for an invoice you don't recognize
Link goes to paypal-resolve.com, paypal-secure.net, or similar fakes
Asks you to install 'support software' to refund

examples.message: PayPal: Pending charge of $487.32 to 'Crypto Trade Inc.' will process in 24 hours. To dispute, call 1-855-555-0118.
examples.reason: PayPal does not include callback numbers in pending-charge emails. The number connects to scammers who guide you through installing remote-access software or 'refunding to yourself.'

examples.message: You have an invoice from John D. for $1,287.40. View invoice: [legitimate-paypal-link]. Questions? Call: 1-800-555-0144
examples.reason: Scammers create real PayPal invoices and abuse the platform to send them. The link itself is to paypal.com, but the phone number in the invoice memo is the scam. Never call numbers inside invoice notes.

what_to_do: Don't call any phone number in a PayPal email.
Open the PayPal app directly. Check 'Activity' — if there's no real pending payment, the email is fake.
If a real invoice is there from a stranger, cancel it from inside PayPal and report.
Forward phishing emails to spoof@paypal.com.
Enable two-factor authentication in PayPal settings.
why_scammers_use: PayPal's reputation lends instant credibility. The 'pending charge' format mimics how PayPal really communicates, and the urgency window pushes panic-calls to scammer-controlled numbers.

faq.q: Can scammers send real PayPal invoices?
faq.a: Yes. PayPal's invoicing system is open. Scammers send real invoices with fake support numbers in the memo. Always verify by checking your PayPal activity directly.

title: Venmo Scams: Unexpected Payments and Refund Traps
meta_description: Got an unexpected Venmo payment from a stranger? Don't refund it. Here's how the scam works and how to protect yourself.
h1: Is the unexpected Venmo payment a scam?
short_answer: Almost certainly yes. The classic Venmo scam: a stranger 'accidentally' sends you money, then asks you to send it back. You refund — and days later their original payment gets reversed (it was from a stolen card), leaving you out the full amount.
red_flags: Unexpected Venmo payment from someone you don't know
Followed by a message saying 'wrong person, please refund'
Pressure to act quickly before they 'get in trouble'
Refund requested to a different account/email than the original sender
Sender's profile is newly created or has no other activity

examples.message: [Payment of $850 received from @newuser_88] — 'Hey, that was meant for someone else, my bad! Can you send it back to @anotheraccount please?'
examples.reason: The original $850 came from a stolen credit card or hacked Venmo account. When the real owner reports fraud, Venmo reverses the original payment. Your 'refund' to @anotheraccount is irreversible — and you're out $850.

what_to_do: Do not send the money back.
Open Venmo → tap the transaction → tap the three-dot menu → Report.
Contact Venmo support directly through the app — they can reverse the original payment safely.
Block the sender.
Wait for Venmo's resolution — never refund directly to the stranger.
why_scammers_use: This scam exploits two facts: (1) most people feel morally obligated to return mistakenly-sent money, and (2) chargeback reversals can take 1-7 days, creating a window where the refund clears before the original payment is voided.

faq.q: Can Venmo recover the money if I already refunded?
faq.a: Sometimes, if reported within 24 hours and the recipient hasn't withdrawn. But Venmo's recovery rate is low — treat refunds to strangers as gone.

title: Cash App 'Money Flip' & Giveaway Scams Explained
meta_description: Promises to multiply your Cash App balance? Free cash from #CashAppFriday? Here's how the scams work and why you'll never get the money.
h1: Is the Cash App money flip / giveaway a scam?
short_answer: Yes, every one of them. There is no such thing as 'Cash App money flipping' — no system multiplies your money. There is no shortcut. People who 'flip' $50 into $500 are running a confidence scam. The official #CashAppFriday giveaways exist but never require you to send money first.
red_flags: Promises to 'flip' $50 into $500, $200 into $2,000, etc.
Asks you to send money first 'to activate' the flip
Uses urgency: 'only 5 spots left,' 'today only'
DM offers from accounts impersonating Cash App or 'verified flippers'
Asks for your Cash App login or PIN under any pretense

examples.message: Hey! I'm a verified Cash App flipper. Send $100 and I'll send back $1,000 in 30 min. Limited time. DM me your $cashtag.
examples.reason: Money does not multiply. After you send, the 'flipper' either disappears or asks for more 'verification' fees. You will never see your money again.

what_to_do: Don't send. There is no legitimate version of this.
Report the account on Cash App, Instagram, or wherever you saw the offer.
Block the account.
If you already sent money: report at cash.app/help. Recovery is rare but always file.
Tell friends — these scams spread by friend-of-friend posts.
why_scammers_use: Money-flip scams target younger users who are familiar with Cash App but unfamiliar with the underlying mechanics. The 'verified flipper' framing borrows authority from real verified accounts.

faq.q: Are any real Cash App giveaways legitimate?
faq.a: The official #CashAppFriday giveaways are real — but they require zero payment from you. If you have to send money first, it's always a scam.

title: eBay Overpayment Scam: How Buyers Trick Sellers
meta_description: Selling on eBay or Craigslist? Buyers who 'overpay' and ask for the difference are running a classic check scam. Here's how to spot it.
h1: Is the eBay buyer who overpaid running a scam?
short_answer: Yes. The 'overpayment' scam works like this: a buyer sends a check (or claims to have wired) more than the asking price, then asks you to refund the difference. The original payment bounces or is reversed days later — and your refund is gone forever.
red_flags: Buyer immediately offers more than asking price
Sends a check, money order, or wire — never PayPal Goods & Services
Asks you to refund the difference to a 'shipping agent' or different account
Pressure to ship quickly before the check clears
Buyer's account is new with little history

examples.message: Hi! My shipping agent will pay you $4,500 — the extra $1,500 covers their fee. Once you receive it, please send $1,500 to the agent at this address. I'll arrange pickup.
examples.reason: The 'check' from the shipping agent is fake or stolen. When it bounces (typically 5-10 days later), the bank reverses it. Your $1,500 to the 'agent' is gone.

what_to_do: Refuse overpayment. Insist on exact amount.
Only accept payment via PayPal Goods & Services or eBay-managed payment.
Wait at least 10 business days for any check to fully clear before shipping or refunding.
Never refund the difference — it's always a scam.
Report the buyer to eBay/marketplace and block.
why_scammers_use: Banks 'provisional credit' for deposited checks within 1-2 days, but a fraudulent check can bounce for up to 30 days. Scammers exploit this gap — by the time the check bounces, the refund and goods are both gone.

faq.q: What if the check seems to clear?
faq.a: Initial credit isn't final. A check can bounce up to a month after deposit. Never act on a check until it's fully verified by your bank manager.

title: DMV Text Scams: Fake License Suspension & Toll Notices
meta_description: Got a text from 'the DMV' about a suspension, toll, or registration issue? Almost certainly a scam. Here's how to verify and respond.
h1: Is the DMV text message a scam?
short_answer: Yes. Your state DMV does not send unsolicited texts about license suspensions, unpaid tolls, or registration renewals. DMV correspondence is by US mail. Any text claiming to be from the DMV with a link to pay is phishing.
red_flags: Text claims your license, registration, or driving privileges will be suspended
Link goes to dmv-payment.com, statedmv.org, or other non-state-gov domains
Demands a small fee or fine ($5-50)
Real state DMV domains end in .gov (e.g., dmv.ca.gov, dmv.ny.gov)
Urgency: 'pay within 24 hours to avoid suspension'

examples.message: [State DMV] Final notice: Your license will be suspended on March 14 due to an unpaid traffic violation of $43.50. Pay now: dmv-payment-portal.us/v
examples.reason: Real DMV citations come by mail. The domain is not a .gov address. The DMV does not suspend licenses by SMS warning.

what_to_do: Don't tap the link.
If you're worried, go to your state's actual DMV website (search for it directly — must end in .gov).
Forward the text to 7726.
Report DMV impersonation to your state attorney general.
Block and delete.
why_scammers_use: Everyone with a car cares about their license. The small payment ($5-50) feels like a fine you'd just pay to avoid hassle — but the goal is your card details for resale.

faq.q: How does the real DMV contact me?
faq.a: By mail. Some states offer email or SMS notifications if you've explicitly signed up, but they never include payment links.

title: Jury Duty Scam Calls: 'Pay or Be Arrested'
meta_description: Got a call saying you missed jury duty and need to pay to avoid arrest? It's a scam. Here's how the script works and what to do.
h1: Is the missed jury duty call a scam?
short_answer: Yes — 100% of the time. No US court demands payment by phone to avoid arrest for missing jury duty. If you actually miss jury duty, real consequences (rare) come by mail with formal court paperwork — never by phone with gift card or wire demands.
red_flags: Caller claims to be a court officer, sheriff's deputy, or US marshal
Says you missed jury duty (you probably never got a real summons)
Demands immediate payment to 'clear the warrant'
Wants payment in gift cards, wire transfer, or cryptocurrency
Threatens arrest if you don't pay in the next hour

examples.message: This is Deputy Sergeant Wilson with the Sheriff's Office. You failed to appear for jury duty on March 3. A warrant has been issued. To avoid arrest, pay $1,500 in Apple gift cards within 90 minutes.
examples.reason: Real arrest warrants are served in person, not avoided by phone payment. Courts never accept gift cards. The script targets fear of arrest and uses fake authority.

what_to_do: Hang up. Do not engage or 'press 1.'
Never read gift card numbers or send wire transfers to anyone over the phone.
If concerned about a real jury summons, call your local court clerk directly (find the number via the court's official .gov website).
Report to reportfraud.ftc.gov and your state attorney general.
Tell anyone older in your family — this scam targets seniors heavily.
why_scammers_use: Fear of arrest is universally motivating. The fake authority + urgent deadline + irreversible payment method (gift cards) creates a panic loop that bypasses rational thinking.

faq.q: What if I actually missed jury duty?
faq.a: You'd receive a written notice by mail. You can call your local court clerk to check. Real consequences are typically a rescheduled date, not arrest.

title: Unemployment Benefits Scam: Fake Claims in Your Name
meta_description: Got a letter or text about unemployment benefits you didn't apply for? Someone may have filed in your name. Here's how to spot it and respond.
h1: Is the unemployment benefits notice a scam?
short_answer: Either you are the victim of identity theft, or the notice itself is phishing. Both are common. If you didn't apply for unemployment, the real risk is that a scammer used your stolen identity to file a fraudulent claim — and is now intercepting the benefits.
red_flags: Letter or email mentions an unemployment claim you didn't file
Debit card arrives in the mail (states often issue benefits via prepaid card)
Tax form 1099-G shows unemployment income you never received
Text or email asks you to 'verify identity' via a link
Phishing variant: emails from state-unemployment.com, jobless-aid.us — not real state .gov domains

examples.message: Your unemployment benefit claim has been approved. Your prepaid debit card with $7,400 in benefits is being mailed.
examples.reason: If you didn't file, someone filed in your name using stolen ID data. They're planning to intercept the card. This is identity theft, not necessarily phishing — but report immediately.

what_to_do: Do NOT activate any debit card that arrives. Doing so confirms the fraud.
Report immediately to your state unemployment office (find via your state .gov site).
File at identitytheft.gov for a federal record and recovery plan.
Place a free credit freeze at Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion.
Notify your employer (they may also need to flag it with payroll).
why_scammers_use: Pandemic-era expansion of unemployment created massive fraud opportunities — state systems weren't designed for the volume and many became targets. Stolen identity data (often from large breaches like Equifax) gets monetized through these fraudulent claims.

faq.q: I never applied. How did this happen?
faq.a: Your SSN, name, and address are likely on breach lists. Scammers cross-reference these to file fraudulent claims. It's not personal — it's industrial fraud.

title: Microsoft Tech Support Scam: Pop-Ups, Calls, and Lock Screens
meta_description: Got a Microsoft warning about a virus, security breach, or 'critical error'? It's a scam. Here's how to recognize and respond safely.
h1: Is the Microsoft tech support warning a scam?
short_answer: Yes, in essentially all cases. Microsoft does not display pop-ups with phone numbers, does not call customers about viruses, and does not lock browsers with sirens or warnings. Every 'Microsoft tech support' phone number you see in a pop-up or hear in a call is a scam.
red_flags: Pop-up appears with a phone number to call
Browser locks up with alarm sound and warning message
Caller claims to be Microsoft and warns of detected viruses
Asks you to install AnyDesk, TeamViewer, or other remote-access tools
Wants you to log into your bank to 'verify' or 'protect' funds

examples.message: CRITICAL SECURITY WARNING: Your computer has been infected with 5 viruses. Personal data is being stolen. Call Microsoft Support immediately: 1-888-555-0193. DO NOT TURN OFF YOUR COMPUTER.
examples.reason: Microsoft never displays such pop-ups. The message is JavaScript on a malicious webpage. Calling the number connects to a scammer who will request remote access and walk you through 'fixing' the computer while draining your bank account.

examples.message: Hello, this is the Microsoft Windows Support Team. We've detected your IP address is sending error reports. Your computer is compromised. Can you please go to your computer so I can help you fix it?
examples.reason: Microsoft does not monitor individual computers or call users about 'error reports.' This is the most-recognized phone scam globally.

what_to_do: Don't call any number in a pop-up.
Don't install remote-access software when prompted by an unsolicited caller.
Force-quit your browser (Cmd+Q on Mac, Alt+F4 on Windows). On mobile, close all tabs.
If the pop-up persists, restart the computer.
Report Microsoft impersonation at microsoft.com/reportascam.
If you already gave remote access: disconnect internet, run a virus scan, change all passwords from a different device, and contact your bank.
why_scammers_use: Microsoft's brand recognition is universal. The pop-up scam works on anyone unfamiliar with how operating systems actually communicate. Once the scammer has remote access, they typically empty bank accounts in 30-60 minutes.

faq.q: Does Microsoft ever call customers?
faq.a: Almost never — and only in response to a request you initiated through official channels. They never cold-call about viruses.

faq.q: I let someone control my computer remotely. What now?
faq.a: Immediately disconnect from internet, change all passwords from another device, contact your bank, and run a full virus scan. Consider taking the computer to a real local technician.

title: McAfee Renewal Scam: Fake Subscription Invoice Emails
meta_description: Got a McAfee renewal email for $300-$500 you didn't authorize? It's a phishing scam. Here's how to spot it.
h1: Is the McAfee renewal email a scam?
short_answer: Yes, in almost all cases. McAfee does not send unsolicited 'auto-renewal' emails with phone numbers to call. The fake invoice is bait — the goal is to get you on the phone with a scammer who will then drain your accounts.
red_flags: Invoice for an amount like $299, $399, $499 — designed to alarm
Includes a callback phone number to 'cancel' — the trap
Sender domain is not @mcafee.com
PDF attachment mimicking an invoice
Subject line uses 'Final Notice' or 'Auto-Renewal Confirmed'

examples.message: McAfee Total Protection Auto-Renewal: $429.99 charged. To cancel, call 1-833-555-0142 within 24 hours.
examples.reason: Real McAfee charges show in your account at mcafee.com. The callback number routes to scammers who walk you through 'refunds' that end in account drainage.

what_to_do: Don't call the number.
Check your bank statement — there won't be a real charge.
Log into mcafee.com directly if you want to verify subscription status.
Report to spam@mcafee.com.
Delete the email.
why_scammers_use: Same playbook as Geek Squad and Norton scams — McAfee is a recognized brand, the fake invoice for hundreds of dollars triggers panic calls, and the phone is where the real fraud happens.

faq.q: What if I have a real McAfee subscription?
faq.a: Verify by logging into mcafee.com directly. Real cancellations happen inside your account.

title: iPhone Virus Popup Scam: 'Your iPhone Has Been Compromised'
meta_description: Saw a scary pop-up on Safari saying your iPhone has a virus? Don't panic. Here's why iPhones don't get viruses and what to do.
h1: Is the iPhone virus warning pop-up a scam?
short_answer: Yes, always. iPhones effectively cannot get viruses through normal use, and Apple does not display warning pop-ups about viruses in Safari. Any pop-up claiming your iPhone is infected, locked, or compromised is a JavaScript trick on a malicious webpage — designed to scare you into installing a fake 'cleaner' app or calling a fake support number.
red_flags: Pop-up appears while browsing Safari
Loud alarm sound or sirens
Tells you your iPhone is locked or all your photos are at risk
Pushes a 'cleaner' or 'security' app from the App Store
Lists a phone number to call for 'Apple Support'

examples.message: WARNING! Your iPhone has been compromised. 14 viruses detected. Tap below to download Apple Security Cleaner now to remove them.
examples.reason: iOS doesn't allow this kind of system warning from Safari. The 'cleaner' app is either fake or a subscription trap. Apple does not warn about viruses this way.

what_to_do: Don't tap any button in the pop-up — not even 'Cancel' or 'Close.'
Close the Safari tab: tap the tabs icon (bottom right), swipe up to close the bad tab.
Clear Safari history: Settings → Safari → Clear History and Website Data.
Don't install any 'cleaner' apps.
If a 'support' phone number was shown, do not call it under any circumstances.
why_scammers_use: iPhones are perceived as ultra-secure, so a 'virus detected' warning feels alarming because it contradicts what people know. Panic = clicks. The follow-up either monetizes through fake subscription apps or routes to phone scammers.

faq.q: Can iPhones get viruses?
faq.a: Effectively no, through normal use. Apple's iOS sandboxing prevents traditional viruses. The only real risk is phishing — handing over credentials voluntarily.

faq.q: Should I install an antivirus app on my iPhone?
faq.a: No. iOS doesn't need one and most iOS 'antivirus' apps don't actually scan anything — they're marketing wrappers around basic phishing protection that Safari already does.

title: Wells Fargo Fraud Alert Text Scam: Real vs Fake
meta_description: Got a Wells Fargo text about fraud, a card alert, or a Zelle issue? Some are real, most are scams. Here's exactly how to tell.
h1: Is the Wells Fargo text a scam?
short_answer: Usually yes. Real Wells Fargo fraud alerts come from short codes (e.g., 93557, 51682) and ask only for a YES/NO reply. They never include a clickable link or a callback number embedded in the message. Any text from Wells Fargo with a link or phone number is a phishing scam.
red_flags: Includes a link to tap
Asks you to call a number embedded in the message
Sender is a regular 10-digit number, not a Wells short code
Asks for your full account number, password, or PIN
Threatens account closure or large transfer reversal

examples.message: Wells Fargo: A $789.34 Zelle to John D. is pending. If unauthorized, call 1-855-555-0192 immediately.
examples.reason: Real Wells Fargo Zelle alerts ask for YES/NO reply, never a callback. The number connects to scammers who 'help' you 'move money to a safe account' (theirs).

examples.message: Wells Fargo Fraud - Did you attempt a $52 charge at Shell Gas? Reply Y if yes, N if no.
examples.reason: Short code sender, YES/NO format, no link, no phone number in the message. Safe to reply Y or N.

what_to_do: Ignore any link or phone number in the message.
Open the Wells Fargo app directly, or call 1-800-869-3557 (the number on your card back).
If you tapped a link and entered credentials, call Wells Fargo immediately and change your password.
Forward suspicious texts to 7726.
Block the sender.
why_scammers_use: Bank fraud alerts have built up trust — customers are used to acting on them quickly. Scammers exploit that trust with lookalike messages that route panic-calls to fraud operators.

faq.q: How does a real Wells Fargo fraud alert look?
faq.a: From a 5-digit short code, asking you to reply Y or N to a specific transaction. No links, no phone numbers in the message itself.

title: Bank of America Text Scam: How to Tell Real from Fake
meta_description: Got a Bank of America text about a charge, Zelle, or fraud alert? Here's how to distinguish real alerts from phishing scams.
h1: Is the Bank of America text a scam?
short_answer: Most likely yes if it contains a link or callback number. Real Bank of America fraud alerts come from short codes and ask for a YES/NO reply — never with a link, never asking you to call a number embedded in the message.
red_flags: Includes a link or callback number
Sender is a regular 10-digit number
Asks for your account number, password, PIN, or OTP
Threatens immediate account action
Uses Bank of America branding but bofa-secure.com type domains

examples.message: Bank of America: Unauthorized login from Texas. Verify identity: bofa-secure-verify.com or call 1-833-555-0177 now.
examples.reason: Real BofA does not include verification links or callback numbers in texts. The domain is fake. Calling the number connects to fraud operators.

what_to_do: Don't tap or call.
Open the BofA app directly, or call 1-800-432-1000 (number on card back).
Forward the text to 7726.
Change your password if you tapped a link and entered anything.
Block and delete.
why_scammers_use: Bank brand recognition + fraud-alert format trains us to respond quickly. Scammers exploit that conditioning with phishing that feels familiar.

faq.q: How does the real BofA contact me about fraud?
faq.a: Short-code SMS with YES/NO reply, an in-app notification, or a phone call to the number on file — never asking you to call a number from a text.

title: Capital One Fraud Alert Scam: Spotting the Fake Texts
meta_description: Capital One alert about an unauthorized charge, Venture transfer, or account access? Here's how to spot the scam version.
h1: Is the Capital One fraud alert a scam?
short_answer: If it has a link or callback number, almost certainly yes. Real Capital One fraud alerts use short codes and ask for a Yes/No reply to a specific transaction. Any embedded link or 'call this number' is phishing.
red_flags: Includes a clickable link
Asks you to call a number embedded in the text
From a regular 10-digit phone, not a Capital One short code
Demands account or password verification
Mentions a charge amount that's just high enough to alarm

examples.message: Capital One: A $1,243 charge at Best Buy was attempted on your card ending 4421. Reply STOP to block or call 1-844-555-0189 to confirm.
examples.reason: Real Capital One alerts use Yes/No reply, not 'call this number.' Replying STOP simply confirms your number is active — and the callback number is the scam's trap.

what_to_do: Ignore the link and phone number.
Open the Capital One app or call 1-800-227-4825 (the number on your card).
Forward to 7726 (SPAM).
If you called and gave info: call Capital One immediately to freeze the card.
Block the sender.
why_scammers_use: Capital One has tens of millions of US customers — high coverage means random recipients are statistically likely to be real customers, lending the scam plausibility.

faq.q: What format do real Capital One alerts use?
faq.a: 5-digit short code, specific transaction details, Yes/No reply. No links, no phone numbers in message.

title: Direct Deposit Change Scam: BEC Attacks on Payroll
meta_description: Did HR get an email from 'you' asking to change your direct deposit account? That's a business email compromise scam — here's how to recognize and prevent it.
h1: Is the direct deposit change email a scam?
short_answer: Yes — if it claims to be from an employee but the email is unfamiliar or oddly worded, it's almost certainly a Business Email Compromise (BEC) attack. Scammers impersonate employees, email HR/payroll asking to redirect direct deposit, and intercept the next paycheck.
red_flags: Email from a slightly off employee address (john.smith@gmaiI.com vs gmail.com)
Casual tone but no prior conversation thread
Requests urgency: 'before this Friday's payroll'
Asks to change to an account that doesn't match employee records
Refuses to call to verify, citing 'in meetings'

examples.message: Hi Linda, I switched banks recently — can you update my direct deposit to this new account before Friday's pay run? Routing 121000358, account 8847291038. Thanks! — Mike
examples.reason: Even if 'Mike' is a real employee, the email is from a spoofed or compromised address. Real Mike's identity should always be verified by phone (using a number you already have) before any payroll change.

what_to_do: Always verify by phone (using a number you already had — not a number in the email) before changing any direct deposit.
Set a policy: no direct deposit changes by email alone, ever.
Use multi-factor confirmation: in-person or video call.
Train all payroll/HR staff on BEC patterns.
If a fraudulent change went through: immediately contact your bank's fraud team — sometimes funds can be recalled within hours.
why_scammers_use: Payroll BEC is one of the highest-yield attacks per attempt: a successful scam captures an entire paycheck, sometimes for months before discovery. Scammers harvest employee names from LinkedIn and compromise or spoof email accounts.

faq.q: Who's responsible if money goes to the scammer's account?
faq.a: Legally complex. Often the employer bears partial liability if they didn't follow proper verification. Banks typically can't reverse the transaction. Prevention is everything.

title: Crypto Recovery Scam: Getting Scammed Twice
meta_description: Already lost money to a crypto scam? Beware of 'recovery agents' promising to get it back — they're almost always a second scam targeting the same victim.
h1: Is the crypto recovery service a scam?
short_answer: Almost certainly yes. After someone loses money to crypto fraud (pig butchering, fake exchange, romance scam), they often get contacted by 'recovery agents' offering to retrieve the funds for an upfront fee. These are second-stage scams targeting already-vulnerable victims. Real recovery is rare and never requires upfront payment.
red_flags: Contact comes via Telegram, WhatsApp, or DM after you've discussed crypto loss publicly
Promises 'guaranteed recovery' or specific success rate
Demands upfront fee before any work begins
Asks for your wallet seed phrase or private keys
Claims insider connections to exchanges or 'blockchain forensics'

examples.type: Telegram DM after a Reddit scam post
examples.message: Hi, I saw your post about losing $50k in the crypto scam. I work with a blockchain recovery firm — we've recovered millions. Our success rate is 85%. Initial retainer is $5,000 to start tracing.
examples.reason: Real recovery firms don't cold-DM victims. No legitimate firm charges upfront retainers for crypto tracing. The recovery 'firm' is the same scammers (or a connected operation) running a second extraction.

what_to_do: Don't pay any upfront fees to anyone promising recovery.
Never share your seed phrase or private keys — that's the keys to your remaining funds, if any.
Report the original scam to ic3.gov and your local FBI office.
If significant funds, hire a licensed attorney (not a 'recovery agent') who can engage real blockchain forensics firms like Chainalysis through proper channels.
Block recovery offers. Be especially skeptical of anyone who messages you about your loss — scammers monitor scam-victim forums.
why_scammers_use: Scam victims are extremely vulnerable to second scams because they're desperate, emotionally compromised, and willing to believe in any path to recovery. The same operations often run both stages.

faq.q: Is any crypto recovery ever real?
faq.a: Real recovery exists but is rare, expensive, and pursued via attorneys + licensed forensics firms — never via cold DM offers.

title: One Ring Callback Scam: Why You Shouldn't Call Back
meta_description: Phone rings once and hangs up? Calling back can cost you hundreds in international charges. Here's how the 'one ring' scam works.
h1: Is the one-ring phone call a scam?
short_answer: Almost always yes. Scammers use auto-dialers to call millions of numbers and hang up after one ring, betting curious people will call back. The numbers connect to premium-rate international lines that charge $20-$30+ per minute — sometimes hundreds of dollars before you realize what's happening.
red_flags: Unknown number calls once and hangs up before voicemail
Caller ID shows an international code: +232 (Sierra Leone), +268 (Eswatini), +809 (Caribbean), +473 (Grenada)
Number looks like a US area code (e.g., 809) but is actually international
Multiple one-ring calls in a row
No legitimate reason a US business would call you from these codes

examples.message: Missed call from +1 (473) 555-0188 — caller hung up after 1 ring at 2:14am.
examples.reason: Area code 473 is Grenada, not the US. Calling back connects to a premium-rate line that charges international rates + premium fees. A 2-minute callback can cost $40+.

what_to_do: Don't call back unknown numbers — ever.
If you're missing a real call, real callers leave voicemails or text.
Block the number.
Check your phone carrier's international block options to prevent these calls reaching you.
